tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

questions.question: How should I pace steps 6–11? The plan says one commit per step and a stop for review after each one.

options.label: One step, then stop (Recommended)
options.description: Implement step 6 with tests, commit it, and stop for your review before step 7. Matches the plan exactly.

options.label: One step, no commit
options.description: Implement each step and leave it uncommitted. You review and commit it yourself before I continue.

options.label: All six, commit each
options.description: Implement steps 6–11 in one go with one commit per step, then stop once for review at the end.

questions.question: Text content can't be identified from bytes alone: any UTF-8 text is valid Markdown, and a .md file can contain HTML tags. How should the server decide between HTML, SVG and Markdown?

options.label: Extension picks, content checks (Recommended)
options.description: Binary types come only from magic bytes. For text, the extension (.html/.htm, .svg, .md/.markdown) chooses the type, and the content must match: valid UTF-8, SVG with an <svg> root, HTML that looks like markup. With no or an unknown extension, sniff the content: <svg> root → SVG, <!doctype html>/<html> → HTML, anything else → reject. Markdown then always needs .md (MCP passes the format explicitly).

options.label: Content only
options.description: Ignore filenames completely. <svg> root → SVG, HTML markers → HTML, any other valid UTF-8 → Markdown. Simpler, but a .txt, .csv or .js file would be accepted and shown as Markdown.

questions.question: PDFs don't render in a sandboxed iframe: Chrome blocks its built-in PDF viewer under `sandbox` (both the iframe attribute and the CSP header), so the plan's approach in §7/S15 doesn't work. How should PDFs be shown?

options.label: pdf.js in the SPA (Recommended)
options.description: Fetch the bytes through the content endpoint and render the pages to canvas with pdfjs-dist (with scripting disabled). Works in every browser and keeps the sandbox CSP on all content. Adds about 1 MB, lazy-loaded only on PDF pages, and the first page doubles as a thumbnail later.

options.label: Unsandboxed iframe for PDF
options.description: Serve PDFs without the CSP sandbox and show them in a plain iframe with the browser's own viewer. Less code, but a different security rule for one type, and the result varies by browser.

options.label: No inline PDF view
options.description: Show a PDF card with Open-in-new-tab and Download only. Simplest, but a weaker review experience.

questions.question: How should I pace steps 6–11? The plan says one commit per step and a stop for review after each one.

options.label: One step, then stop (Recommended)
options.description: Implement step 6 with tests, commit it, and stop for your review before step 7. Matches the plan exactly.

options.label: One step, no commit
options.description: Implement each step and leave it uncommitted. You review and commit it yourself before I continue.

options.label: All six, commit each
options.description: Implement steps 6–11 in one go with one commit per step, then stop once for review at the end.

questions.question: Text content can't be identified from bytes alone: any UTF-8 text is valid Markdown, and a .md file can contain HTML tags. How should the server decide between HTML, SVG and Markdown?

options.label: Extension picks, content checks (Recommended)
options.description: Binary types come only from magic bytes. For text, the extension (.html/.htm, .svg, .md/.markdown) chooses the type, and the content must match: valid UTF-8, SVG with an <svg> root, HTML that looks like markup. With no or an unknown extension, sniff the content: <svg> root → SVG, <!doctype html>/<html> → HTML, anything else → reject. Markdown then always needs .md (MCP passes the format explicitly).

options.label: Content only
options.description: Ignore filenames completely. <svg> root → SVG, HTML markers → HTML, any other valid UTF-8 → Markdown. Simpler, but a .txt, .csv or .js file would be accepted and shown as Markdown.

questions.question: PDFs don't render in a sandboxed iframe: Chrome blocks its built-in PDF viewer under `sandbox` (both the iframe attribute and the CSP header), so the plan's approach in §7/S15 doesn't work. How should PDFs be shown?

options.label: pdf.js in the SPA (Recommended)
options.description: Fetch the bytes through the content endpoint and render the pages to canvas with pdfjs-dist (with scripting disabled). Works in every browser and keeps the sandbox CSP on all content. Adds about 1 MB, lazy-loaded only on PDF pages, and the first page doubles as a thumbnail later.

options.label: Unsandboxed iframe for PDF
options.description: Serve PDFs without the CSP sandbox and show them in a plain iframe with the browser's own viewer. Less code, but a different security rule for one type, and the result varies by browser.

options.label: No inline PDF view
options.description: Show a PDF card with Open-in-new-tab and Download only. Simplest, but a weaker review experience.

content.text:
Step 6 is committed as `0f2c03d`, "Add StorageDriver abstraction with an atomic local driver". Typecheck, lint, Prettier, the unit tests (67) and the e2e tests (31) all pass, and the running dev stack's `/api/health` reports `{"database":"up","storage":"up"}`.

**What's in it**
- **`apps/api/src/storage/`:** the `StorageDriver` interface from §5 and the `LocalStorageService` driver. `STORAGE_DRIVER` chooses the driver. `s3` and `azure` stop the app at boot with a clear "not implemented" message instead of having stub classes.
- **Atomic writes:** each upload streams into a `*.tmp` file, is flushed to disk, and is renamed into place; the directory is then synced on a best-effort basis. The SHA-256 and size are computed while streaming. If the stream fails partway or the size doesn't match what was expected, nothing is left on disk.
- **Immutable blobs:** writing to a key that already exists is refused.
- **Key safety:** keys are generated by the server (`artifacts/{artifactId}/{versionNo}-{uuid}`) and must match a strict pattern: no dots, no empty segments, no backslashes. The resolved path must also stay inside the storage root. Tests cover attempts to escape the root and confirm nothing outside it is touched.
- **`/api/health`:** it now also writes and deletes a small test blob. The database and storage checks run in parallel, each with a timeout, and the 503 response says which check failed.
- **New env vars:**
  - `STORAGE_DRIVER` defaults to `local`.
  - `STORAGE_LOCAL_ROOT` defaults to `.data/blobs` in development, which is already ignored by git and Docker. The e2e tests use `.data/test-blobs`.
  - In production, `STORAGE_LOCAL_ROOT` is required so blobs never quietly go into the container's own disk and get lost on redeploy. The production image sets it to `/data/blobs`.

**Worth a look when you review**
- **Error classes:** `BlobNotFoundError` and the other storage errors are in `storage.errors.ts`. CLAUDE.md's rule about the `.types.ts` file covers types and interfaces, not classes, so I kept them separate.
- **Railway volume permissions:** the production image creates `/data/blobs` owned by the `node` user. Railway volumes may mount as root, which could make `/data` unwritable. If so, the health check will show it as a 503 on storage. I haven't verified this; it's for when the deploy happens.
- **Leftover temp files:** `*.tmp` files left by a crash are removed by the sweeper in step 23. The sweeper will also need a way to list stored files, which I'll add to the interface then.

Next is step 7: content validation, using the "extension picks, content checks" rule for text formats and writing that rule into the plan. Tell me when to go ahead.

lines: The web UI and MCP use the same pipeline:

1. **Receive:** multipart with busboy/multer `limits.fileSize = MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES`, or MCP inline text `content` (byte length checked before processing), or the raw-body `PUT` to an upload session (streamed with the same limit). Anything over the limit gets `413 ARTIFACT_TOO_LARGE`.

-2. **Validate type:** sniff magic bytes (`file-type`) for binary formats; for text formats, check UTF-8 and structure (HTML/SVG/Markdown). Compare against the allowlist: `text/html`, `image/svg+xml`, `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/webp`, `image/gif`, `application/pdf`, `text/markdown`. The **server** decides the MIME type; the client's claim is ignored.

+2. **Validate type:** the allowlist is `text/html`, `image/svg+xml`, `text/markdown`, `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/webp`, `image/gif`, `application/pdf`. The **server** decides the MIME type from the first 64 KB of content; the client's `Content-Type` is ignored.
+   - **Binary formats** come from magic bytes (`file-type`) only. The filename is ignored, and any other detected binary type (zip, executables, …) is rejected.

+   - **Text formats** must be UTF-8 throughout, with no NUL bytes (checked as the content streams). Bytes alone can't tell them apart (any text is valid Markdown, and Markdown may contain HTML), so the **extension picks and the content must match**: `.md`/`.markdown` → Markdown (any text); `.html`/`.htm` → HTML (must start with markup); `.svg` → SVG (must have an `<svg>` root; DOCTYPEs with an internal subset are rejected). MCP passes the format explicitly instead of a filename.

+   - **No or another extension:** only an unmistakable SVG (`<svg>` root) or HTML document (`<!doctype html>` / `<html>`) is accepted; Markdown always needs `.md` or an explicit format, so `.txt`, `.csv`, `.js` etc. are rejected.
3. **Store blob** under a fresh key, with the hash computed while streaming.
4. **Idempotency check** (section 10): if this owner already published the same `sha256` (or the target's current version has it), return the existing result.
5. **DB transaction:** `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` the artifact → insert the version with `latest_version_no + 1` → update `current_version_id`. Commit.
6. ✅ `StorageDriver` with the local driver, plus unit tests.
-7. Content validation (type sniffing, allowlist, streaming size limit), plus unit tests.
+7. ✅ Content validation (type sniffing, allowlist, streaming size limit), plus unit tests.

content.text:
Step 7 is done and the changes are in the working tree, not committed. From now on I'll only commit when you ask. Typecheck, lint, Prettier, the API build, the unit tests (106, up from 67) and the e2e tests (31) all pass.

**What's in it**
- **Shared allowlist** (`packages/shared/src/artifacts.ts`): the text formats with their MIME types, the binary MIME types, and `artifactMimeTypeSchema`. The web app will use these for the upload picker and the viewers.
- **`detectContentType(head, hint)`** in `uploads/content/detect-content-type.ts`, following the rule you chose:
  - Binary formats are decided by magic bytes only. Zip files, executables and other detected binaries are rejected, even with a `.png` or `.md` name.
  - Text must be UTF-8 with no NUL bytes. The extension (or MCP's explicit format) picks the type, and the content has to match: `.md` accepts any text, `.html` must start with markup, `.svg` needs an `<svg>` root.
  - Without a known extension, only a full SVG or HTML document is accepted. `.txt`, `.csv` and `.js` are rejected.
  - Empty files are rejected.
  - Error messages are readable, e.g. *"The file does not contain an SVG image. Supported formats: …"*, and list the allowed types in `details`.
- **`ContentInspectorService.inspect(source, hint)`**: reads the first 64 KB, decides the type, and returns `{ mimeType, body }`.
  - `body` streams the whole content, enforcing `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` (`ARTIFACT_TOO_LARGE`) and checking UTF-8 across chunk boundaries for text formats.
  - When a check fails or the reader gives up, the source stream is destroyed. If a check fails while the body is going into storage, nothing is left on disk; a test runs this against the real local driver.
- **New env var:** `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES`, 10 MB by default.
- **`UploadsModule`** exports the inspector. Nothing imports it yet; step 8 will.
- **Test fixtures:** small files with real magic bytes, in `test/fixtures/content.ts`, so step 8's e2e tests can reuse them.
- **Plan §6, step 2** now spells out the text-detection rule, and step 7 is marked ✅.

**Worth a look when you review**
- **SVG DOCTYPEs:** an SVG whose DOCTYPE declares its own entities (`<!DOCTYPE svg [<!ENTITY …>]>`) is rejected, to rule out entity-expansion tricks. Real SVG exports don't use these.
- **Regex safety:** the detection regexes are written so a malformed file can't make them run for a long time, and a test checks they stay fast on large runs of whitespace.
- **Dev container:** `file-type` is a new dependency. Run `pnpm dev:docker` once step 8 wires the module in, because the container's `node_modules` comes from its image.

A commit message, if you want one: *"Add content validation: type detection by magic bytes and extension rules, streaming size limit and UTF-8 check"*.

Next is step 8: create an artifact with v1, get one, list mine, and an owner-only `AccessPolicy`.

message.content: why is @apps/api/src/uploads/content/detect-content-type.ts a bunch of functions and not a class?

content.text:
I chose functions because detection is stateless: bytes plus a hint go in, a MIME type comes out. There's no configuration, no dependencies and nothing to remember between calls. The API already handles stateless logic this way: `parseEnv` in `config/env.ts`, `isUniqueViolation` in `database/postgres-errors.ts`, `buildLoggerParams` in `common/logging/logger.config.ts`. Classes are used where there's state (`ByteMeter`, `Utf8Validator`) or where Nest injection is needed (`ContentInspectorService`). The service is the injectable entry point, and detection is a pure step inside it, so it can be tested directly without building a Nest module or mocks.

A class would make sense in either of these cases:
- **It needs injected config.** For example, if the allowed types became configurable through env, an `@Injectable() ContentTypeDetectorService` reading `Env` would be the right shape.
- **Callers need to replace it in tests.** Today nothing does. The inspector tests use real detection on real fixture bytes, which is what I'd want.

While re-reading the file, I noticed a real problem with it as it stands. `unsupported()` is exported from here and imported by `utf8-validator.ts`, so the validator depends on the detection module just to build an error. It's an error factory and should live in its own small file, e.g. `uploads/content/unsupported-type.error.ts`, which both files import. I'd fix that whichever way we go.

My recommendation is to keep detection as functions, consistent with `parseEnv` and `isUniqueViolation`, and move `unsupported()` out. If you'd rather have a single rule that domain logic in `apps/api` is always a class, I'll turn it into a `ContentTypeDetector` class and add the rule to CLAUDE.md so later steps follow it. git add -A && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Add content validation: type detection, streaming size limit and UTF-8 check

- Shared allowlist of artifact MIME types (text formats and binary formats)
- detectContentType: binary formats from magic bytes only (file-type),
  ignoring the filename; other detected binaries are rejected
- Text formats must be UTF-8 without NUL bytes; the extension (or MCP's
  explicit format) picks HTML, SVG or Markdown and the content must match;
  without one, only a full SVG or HTML document is accepted, so Markdown
  always needs .md; SVG DOCTYPEs with an internal subset are rejected
- ContentInspectorService reads the first 64 KB to decide the type, then
  streams the full body with MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES and UTF-8 enforced (ByteMeter,
  Utf8Validator); a failure destroys the source and leaves no blob in storage
- UNSUPPORTED_TYPE errors list the supported formats; ARTIFACT_TOO_LARGE
  names the limit
- New env: MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES (default 10 MB)
- Plan §6 documents the text-detection rule
- Unit tests for detection, the inspector (with the local driver), the byte
  meter and the UTF-8 validator; shared content fixtures in test/fixtures

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Step 8 is implemented and the changes are uncommitted. Typecheck, lint, Prettier and the API build pass, as do the API unit tests (151) and e2e tests (52). I also tried publish, get and list against the running app through the Vite proxy. To do that I ran `pnpm dev:docker`, which rebuilt and restarted your dev containers: the API container had stopped compiling because its image didn't have the new `busboy` dependency. The smoke-test user and its blob are deleted.

**API**
- **`POST /api/artifacts`:** multipart with a `metadata` JSON field first, then exactly one `file` part.
  - The file streams straight through type detection and the size limit into storage; nothing is buffered in memory.
  - A `Content-Length` over the limit gets a 413 before anything is read.
  - If the client disconnects mid-upload, the storage write fails instead of hanging.
  - If the database transaction fails, the stored blob is deleted again.
- **`GET /api/artifacts/:id`:** owner only. Other users, missing IDs and malformed IDs all get the same 404.
- **`GET /api/artifacts?scope=mine&limit=&cursor=`:** your published artifacts, newest first, paged with an opaque cursor.
- **`AccessPolicyService`:** owner-only for now. Deleted artifacts are hidden from everyone. Denials are logged at debug with IDs and a reason. Its `FORBIDDEN` branch ("can view but can't edit") only becomes reachable in step 12.
- **Publish logs:** each publish logs received → type detected → blob stored (bytes, ms) → version committed.

**Data and shared code**
- **Migration:** creates `artifacts` and `artifact_versions` with enum types and the circular `current_version_id` foreign key.
  - A new artifact is inserted as a draft and switched to published once its version exists. A CHECK constraint enforces that a published artifact always has a version.
  - The `artifacts` timestamps use millisecond precision so the list cursor matches rows exactly.
- **Shared zod schemas:**

message.content: why did we go with cursor pagination and not simple page based one?

content.text:
I went with a cursor because of how this list is sorted. I listed it as a default before starting, but didn't explain why, so here is the reasoning.

**Why a cursor fits here**
- **The sort key moves.** The gallery is ordered by `updated_at`, and artifacts get updated while someone is browsing: metadata edits, new versions (step 11) and especially the AI job (step 25), which rewrites metadata seconds after every publish. With `OFFSET`, each of those moves items between pages, so "load more" shows duplicates or silently skips items. A cursor continues after a fixed `(updated_at, id)` position, so nothing is repeated or lost.
- **It matches the UI.** The plan's gallery is a card grid that loads more as you scroll, and MCP's `find_artifacts` lets an agent fetch the next page. Neither needs to jump to page 7.
- **Performance is a minor reason.** `OFFSET n` reads and throws away `n` rows, while the cursor reads straight from the `(owner_id, updated_at DESC, id DESC)` index. That matters at scale but not for a demo.

**What it costs**
- **No page numbers.** You can't show "page 3 of 12" or jump to a page, and there's no total count unless we add a separate `COUNT(*)`.
- **More moving parts.** The opaque cursor encoding, and millisecond timestamps so the cursor compares exactly. Plain offset paging needs neither.
- **Step 15 gets harder.** Search results sorted by relevance would need a cursor on the computed rank, which is awkward. The simpler route there is to sort search results by relevance and use a plain limit or offset, since that sort key doesn't change while you page.

I'd keep the cursor for the gallery lists, mainly because the AI job reorders items right after publishing, and use simpler paging for search in step 15. If you'd rather have numbered pages in the gallery, switching to `page`/`pageSize` with a total count is a small change now, as long as you accept the duplicates and skips described above.

content.text:
The artifacts list now uses numbered pages. Nothing is committed. Typecheck, lint and Prettier pass, as do the unit tests (148; four fewer now that the cursor tests are gone) and the e2e tests (59).

- **API:** `GET /api/artifacts?scope=mine&page=1&pageSize=24` returns `{ items, page, pageSize, total }`.
  - `page` starts at 1 and is capped at 1000, so a client can't make the database skip an unlimited number of rows.
  - `pageSize` defaults to 24 and is capped at 50.
  - A page past the end returns no items, but still includes `total`.
- **Service:** `ArtifactsService.list(actor, { ownerId?, page, pageSize })` returns `{ items, total }`. The access filter from the last change still applies before any other filter. Sorting by `updated_at` then `id` keeps each page's contents stable when timestamps tie.
- **Removed:** `list-cursor.ts` and its spec, the cursor types, and the millisecond-precision timestamps, which only existed for the cursor.
- **Migration:** I changed the uncommitted migration in place. Your dev database had already applied it, so I reverted it there first and re-applied the new version. The test database is rebuilt from scratch on each e2e run.
- **Plan §13** now lists `page=&pageSize=`.
- **e2e tests** cover paging with totals, an empty page past the end, the defaults, the access check with another user's `ownerId` (which now returns `total: 0`), and five invalid `page`/`pageSize` values.

As we discussed, an artifact updated while someone is browsing (and the AI job in step 25 updates every new artifact shortly after publish) can move between pages. Moving from page 1 to page 2 can then show an item twice or skip one. Page-number paging always has this trade-off; it just matters more because the list is sorted by last update.

content.text: Step 9 is implemented and the changes are uncommitted. Step 8 was committed as `3c83075` before I started. Typecheck, lint, Prettier and the web build pass, as do all the tests: API unit (163), shared (25), web (48) and API e2e (65). I couldn't look at the viewers in a real browser because none is installed here. What I did check against the running dev stack: the content endpoint's headers, the download filename, the 304 on revalidation, the `/artifacts/:id` route, and that the lazy-loaded viewer modules compile in Vite. Things worth checking by eye: - that a PDF renders through pdf.js - that HTML using a CDN (e.g. Tailwind) is styled inside the iframe - that Full screen works You'd need to publish with curl for now, since the publish dialog arrives in step 10. The steps are signup → `POST /api/artifacts` with `-F 'metadata={"title":"x"}' -F file=@x.pdf` → open `/artifacts/`. **API** - **`GET /api/artifacts/:id/versions/:no/content`:** - Only people who can view the artifact get the content; anyone else, and any missing or malformed version number, gets a 404. - Every response carries the sandbox CSP you approved (external https resources allowed; fetch, forms, nested frames and `` blocked; only the app can frame it), plus `nosniff`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. - Text formats are served with `charset=utf-8`. - The content hash is the `ETag` with `Cache-Control: private, no-cache`, so the browser revalidates every time and gets a cheap 304, always after the access check. - `?download=1` sends `Content-Disposition: attachment`. The name is the original filename or the title, with an extension matching the real type, and works for non-ASCII names. - The route writes the response itself, because Nest would otherwise reset the 304 to a 200. - **`formatBytes`** moved into the shared package. `ByteMeter` uses it, and so does the web app. Limits under 1 KB now read "100 B" instead of "1 KB". **Web** - **`/artifacts/:id` page:** title, owner, version, type and size, last updated, a Private/Public badge, description and tags. - Download and Full screen buttons. Full screen uses the browser's Fullscreen API on the in-app viewer rather than opening the raw URL, because a sandboxed PDF wouldn't render there. - States for not found (shown once, no retry on 404), a draft with no content yet, and errors. - **Viewers:** - HTML: an iframe sandboxed with `allow-scripts allow-popups` only. - PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF and SVG: ``. For SVG this differs from the plan, which used an iframe; inside `` an SVG's scripts can never run. - Markdown: react-markdown with tables (GFM). Raw HTML in the source is shown as text and `javascript:` links are dropped. Links open in a new tab with `noopener noreferrer`. - PDF: pdf.js, rendering up to 100 pages to canvases. - The Markdown and PDF viewers load lazily, which brought the main bundle from 799 KB down to 510 KB. - **Supporting pieces:** - `apiFetchContent`, the API client's counterpart for non-JSON content, using the same error handling. - A relative-time formatter and the shadcn `Badge`. - The test fake grew into `installFakeApi`, which also serves artifacts and their content. **Plan updates:** §7 and S15 now describe the final CSP, the SVG-as-image choice, pdf.js and Full screen. Step 9 is marked ✅. **Worth a look when you review** - **Dev stack:** I ran `pnpm dev:docker` again, because the web container didn't have the new packages. - **Revocation and caching:** revalidating on every view keeps revocation immediate, at the cost of one request per view. Each request returns a 304 without reading the file from storage. - **No byte-range support:** the content endpoint doesn't support HTTP byte ranges yet; pdf.js downloads the whole file, which is fine at the 10 MB limit. Suggested commit message: *"Add the sandboxed content endpoint and an artifact page with a viewer per type"*.

content.text: On the server, yes. In the browser, it depends on the type. **Server (all types):** `GET /api/artifacts/:id/versions/:no/content` streams straight from storage to the response with `pipeline(fileStream, res)`, so the file is never loaded into the API's memory. It sets `Content-Length` up front. On repeat views the browser sends the `ETag` and gets a 304 with no body, so storage isn't read again. One gap: there's no support for byte ranges (`Range` requests), so every request gets the whole file. **Browser, per viewer:** | Type | How it loads | Renders as bytes arrive? | |---|---|---| | HTML | the `
